Treatise
trē´tĭs
n. (a written composition handling a subject in order; Luke's word for his own Gospel)
Old French traitis, from Latin tractare, to handle. The AV uses it once, and it is Luke describing the third Gospel to Theophilus (Act 1:1).

Biblical Definition

A treatise is an ordered written account. Luke opens Acts by naming his Gospel one: “The former treatise have I made, O Theophilus, of all that Jesus began both to do and teach” (Act 1:1). His preface describes the method — many had taken in hand to set forth in order a declaration, and he, “having had perfect understanding of all things from the very first, to write unto thee in order”, that Theophilus “mightest know the certainty of those things, wherein thou hast been instructed” (Luk 1:3–4). John states his own purpose: “these are written, that ye might believe that Jesus is the Christ” (John 20:31), and concedes the limit: “the world itself could not contain the books that should be written” (John 21:25). Paul, in prison, sends for “the books, but especially the parchments” (2Ti 4:13).

Webster 1828 Definition

Webster (1828) defines treatise as a tract; a written composition on a particular subject, in which the principles of it are discussed or explained.

expand to see more

TREATISE, n. A tract; a written composition on a particular subject, in which the principles of it are discussed or explained.

A treatise implies more form and method than an essay, but may be without the formality of a regular system.

Key Scripture

Act 1:1 — "The former treatise have I made, O Theophilus, of all that Jesus began both to do and teach,"

Luk 1:3 — "It seemed good to me also, having had perfect understanding of all things from the very first, to write unto thee in order, most excellent Theophilus,"

John 20:31 — "But these are written, that ye might believe that Jesus is the Christ, the Son of God; and that believing ye might have life through his name."

John 21:25 — "And there are also many other things which Jesus did, the which, if they should be written every one, I suppose that even the world itself could not contain the books that should be written. Amen."

2Ti 4:13 — "The cloke that I left at Troas with Carpus, when thou comest, bring with thee, and the books, but especially the parchments."

Modern Corruption

Inspiration is imagined as dictation, and Luke describes research, sources and an editorial plan.

expand to see more

Luke's preface is the most valuable four verses in the New Testament on how Scripture came to be, and it describes ordinary historical labour. Many had taken in hand to set forth a declaration; eyewitnesses and ministers of the word had delivered them; Luke had perfect understanding of all things from the very first; and he determined to write in order. Research, sources, arrangement, an intended reader and a stated purpose — and the result is inspired Scripture. Inspiration in the Reformed account does not bypass the writer's mind, temperament, vocabulary or method; it governs the outcome, so that what Luke wrote by investigation is exactly what God said.

That is why the Gospels differ in arrangement without contradicting, why Luke reads like a physician and Mark like a man in a hurry, and why John states an editorial principle openly — many other signs truly did Jesus, which are not written in this book; but these are written, that ye might believe. A selection was made, on purpose, for an effect. Recognising this protects the text from two opposite errors: the reader who is scandalised to find design in it, and the reader who treats the design as evidence that the content is invented.

Second Timothy 4:13 is the small human detail that belongs beside all this. Paul is near the end, in a cold prison, and what he asks for is a cloak, the books, and especially the parchments. The man who wrote a third of the New Testament wanted something to read. That is a reasonable rebuke to any Christian who supposes that a spiritual man has outgrown study, and a fair description of what this dictionary is for: an ordered handling of words, so that what is already written may be better understood.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

Greek logos (G3056), account, word, treatise; anatassomai (G392), to draw up in order; kathexes (G2517), in order, consecutively; membrana (G3200), parchment.

expand to see more

Greek proton logon (G3056) — the former treatise, the first account; Acts 1:1.

Greek kathexes (G2517) — in order, one after another; Luke 1:3, Acts 11:4, 18:23.

Greek biblia / membranas (G975, G3200) — the books, especially the parchments; 2 Timothy 4:13.

Usage

"“The former treatise have I made, O Theophilus” — Luke, of his own Gospel."

"“To write unto thee in order” — research, sources, and a plan."

"“The books, but especially the parchments” — asked for from a prison."
